overview: At 100 CE, the Southern Xiongnu lived inside a dangerous bargain. Their chanyu ruled through royal kin and marriage clans, guarded Han’s northern frontier and received grain, livestock, silk and gold, while Han officials watched him and elite sons went to Luoyang as hostages. This was not the enormous empire of earlier Xiongnu rulers. It was a smaller, divided world of herders, cavalry, markets, forts, farm country and families navigating two political traditions. Rebellions repeatedly shook the alliance. Xianbei power rose independently across the outer steppe, and a disastrous 177 expedition proved that yesterday’s great name did not guarantee tomorrow’s victory. In 188 rebels killed the chanyu; in 216 Cao Cao replaced his office with Five Divisions under imperial supervision. Yet people did not evaporate when the title ended. Communities continued in Ordos and Shanxi, joining Wei and Jin armies, courts and economies. The atlas makes the story trickier: its polygon sits far west around Alxa, missing the documented settlement core. Read it as a locator with a warning label, not a hoofprint-perfect border.

periods.title: Rebellion, bargaining and a repaired alliance
periods.summary: Northern refugees and Southern leaders tested Han control; the 109 to 110 rising failed, and Xiongnu auxiliaries soon served Han again against the Qiang.

periods.title: Xianbei pressure and authority in retreat
periods.summary: A 124 mutiny and the great 140 revolt revealed a shrinking chanyu’s reach. Han withdrew from much of the Ordos while rivals and local leaders gained room.

periods.title: Court-appointed chanyus under a stronger Xianbei sky
periods.summary: Han officials restored compliant chanyus, but the office carried less practical power while Tanshihuai built an independent Xianbei confederation across the outer steppe.

periods.title: The failed northern expedition and open fragmentation
periods.summary: A Han army with Southern Xiongnu cavalry suffered disaster against Tanshihuai in 177. Rival clans, including the Xiuchuge, increasingly mattered more than the chanyu.

periods.title: A murdered chanyu and wandering claimants
periods.summary: Xiuchuge rebels killed Qiangqu; Yufuluo and Huchuquan survived amid Han civil war, but the old confederate office no longer commanded its former communities.

periods.title: Five Divisions under Cao Wei
periods.summary: Cao Cao kept Huchuquan at court and organized Xiongnu groups into five supervised divisions. This was administrative survival under Wei, not a restored Southern Xiongnu state.

periods.title: Western Jin settlements and new elite pathways
periods.summary: Western Jin inherited the divisions around Taiyuan and the Fen valley. Some leaders entered court service and classical learning while frontier unrest continued.

sections.title: First, inspect what the atlas actually draws

items.text: The exact record is southern-xiongnu, labelled “Southern Xiongnu” and indexed circa 100 to 300 CE. Coverage records two intervals, 100 to 200 and 200 to 300, and showed no card before this packet. The dates describe imported map coverage, not the polity’s birth and death certificates or a modern territorial claim.

At both 100 and 200 the target is one Polygon with one ring and 20 coordinate positions. Its bounds are [98.29358293582936, 39.41380788564797, 106.35766357663579, 42.82299046120785], and both coordinates hash to eb99737ebad52a00066b46c0925c947a0a38598b34652faa036b2a83bb48bfca. The repeated outline is exact, not an estimate from a screenshot.

Point tests put Ejin/Khara-Khoto, the Badain Jaran and northern Alxa inside, but Ordos, Hohhot, Shuofang, Datong, Taiyuan, Pingyang, Ye and Luoyang outside. Historical sources place Southern Xiongnu communities around Ordos and later Shanxi, so the polygon is seriously displaced westward.

The same snapshots draw Han over Ordos, Hohhot, Shuofang, Datong, Taiyuan and Pingyang. Overlapping labels can be useful, because Southern Xiongnu communities lived within Han frontier commanderies; here, however, the target polygon misses those tested settlements instead of showing the political overlap.

The target vanishes at 300 and remains absent at 400. Jin and the separate han-zhao feature appear in different places, while the exact Southern Xiongnu shape is gone. That seam is an atlas decision: Cao Cao ended the chanyu office in 216, and Han-Zhao began only after Liu Yuan’s revolt in 304.

sections.title: A southern branch formed before this map begins

items.text: Bi broke with the northern ruler Punu, established an Ordos base, and took the chanyu title in winter 48/49. In spring 50 he secured Han alliance, moved his headquarters to Meiji in western Ordos and accepted close supervision. The atlas begins half a century later.

At the split, Bi could claim only eight tribal divisions and perhaps 100,000 people. Han valued them as a frontier buffer, but subsidies, an official supervisor and a chanyu’s son held at Luoyang made the bargain unequal. “Ally,” “vassal” and “hostage” all belong in the same complicated sentence.

The court history says the new chanyu received a seal, carriage, weapons, silk, grain, cattle and sheep, while clerks and guards attended his camp. These were resources for an elite political system and its followers. They are not a shopping list for every family on the frontier.

Southern forces joined Han campaigns that destroyed the northern royal line in 89 to 92. Xianbei groups then occupied much former northern territory. That makes three distinct histories: the older imperial confederation, the Han-aligned Southern polity and a rising Xianbei world, not one people changing labels on command.

The earlier atlas ids xiongnu and xiongnu-bc200 remain separate. Southern Xiongnu is absent at 100 BCE and 1 BCE, then appears at 100 CE; no appliesTo alias is added. The card can explain institutional inheritance without swallowing two earlier histories or borrowing their enormous steppe borders.

sections.title: Politics ran through kin, gifts and watchful neighbors

items.text: The chanyu’s royal clan and four leading non-royal houses were tied by marriage. Ranked “horn” princes stood in a succession order, while other offices varied with power and the number of followers. This was government through people and relationships, not departments neatly filed in identical tents.

The same Chinese account says Huyan, Lan and Xubu nobles heard cases and reported decisions orally to the chanyu, without written dockets. That detail describes an outsider’s view of elite justice. It does not prove that nobody remembered precedents, used marks, negotiated locally or disagreed with a verdict.

Each New Year, the chanyu sent memorials and hostages; Han returned gold, silk and prized foods distributed among the queen mother, consorts, princes and senior lords. Gifts held the coalition together, but the named recipients also reveal rank. Diplomacy could arrive wrapped in brocade and political obligation.

Frontier markets mattered as much as battlefields. In 84, Northern Xiongnu traders reportedly brought more than ten thousand cattle and horses; Southern forces then attacked them for captives and livestock. Trade, raiding and alliance were competing ways to obtain resources, sometimes in the same season.

Later Han control increasingly depended on bargaining: Xiongnu and Wuhuan auxiliaries defended districts where Han civilian populations had fallen. A chanyu could receive imperial backing yet fail to command every clan. Calling the Southern polity a simple puppet misses both coercion and the room local leaders still had.

sections.title: Rebellions and Xianbei power changed the frontier

items.text: Northern refugees rebelled in 94, and in 109 the Southern chanyu joined a rising during the great Qiang war; by 110 it had failed. Xiongnu units later fought again for Han, and another mutiny came in 124. Loyalty was repeatedly renegotiated, not permanently switched on in 50.

In 140 a Southern Xiongnu revolt spread across the frontier. Han officials blamed the chanyu Xiuli for failing to control it; pressured and humiliated, he killed himself. Han then abandoned much of the Ordos. The episode shows how a title could survive even while its practical reach collapsed.

Tanshihuai united a powerful Xianbei coalition across the northern steppe. In 177, a Han expedition including Southern Xiongnu cavalry followed him too far and suffered a crushing defeat; sources claim three quarters did not return. Xianbei were independent rivals and occasional partners, never an alias for Southern Xiongnu.

Archaeology adds another warning. Scholars note that named Xiongnu events or communities can rarely be matched securely to a material “Xiongnu culture.” Mixed graves near a fluid frontier may show interaction without supplying the deceased person’s political membership. Pottery is excellent evidence and a terrible passport.

In 188, Xiuchuge mutineers killed chanyu Qiangqu. His son Yufuluo sought help, but Han itself dissolved into civil war; refused a stable return, he became a wandering military leader until 195. Huchuquan inherited the claim, not a reunited confederation. Fragmentation had become the political reality.

sections.title: The chanyu office ended, but people did not

items.text: The Xiuchuge submitted to Cao Cao in 214. In 216 he kept Huchuquan at court and installed Qubei over five divisions along the southern Ordos and Shanxi frontier. No new chanyu followed Huchuquan. That is the strongest political endpoint for the Southern Xiongnu state inside this atlas interval.

Cao Wei’s Five Divisions were an administrative framework for communities already fragmented by war and migration. Leaders could serve imperial armies, bargain for rank or resist. The arrangement preserved group names and organization under another government; it did not restore the old chanyu’s sovereignty with a new office sign.

The later Jin history places five Xiongnu divisions around the Fen River and Jinyang during the Taikang era of the 280s. That is far east and south of the atlas polygon. It supports a Shanxi settlement story, but the text was compiled centuries later and favors elite political lineages.

Liu Yuan appears in the same later source as a Xiongnu elite educated in the Poetry, Documents, Changes, Zuo tradition, histories and military texts while linked to the Jin court. This is striking evidence for one aristocrat’s learned path, not a school timetable for every Southern Xiongnu child.

Liu Yuan founded his own Han regime only in 304, after this card ends; the atlas represents Han-Zhao separately at 300 to 400. Descent claims gave the later court legitimacy, but successor identity is not uninterrupted statehood. The 216 office ending and the 304 rebellion belong on opposite sides of that distinction.

sections.title: Herds, grain, markets and the work behind them

items.text: Pastoralism remained fundamental: households and followers managed horses, sheep, goats and cattle, moving skills and animals through a frontier of pastures, forts and farms. Earlier Xiongnu states also used agriculture. The balance varied by place; “mobile” never meant nobody planted grain or stayed beside a town.

Elite gifts of cattle, sheep, grain and silk were political fuel. Keeping, dividing, transporting and redistributing them required herders, drovers, cooks, guards, weavers and storekeepers whom the court text rarely names. A royal list proves resources changed hands; it cannot calculate an ordinary household’s yearly income.

Earlier and mostly northern Xiongnu isotope studies find millet alongside animal foods, showing a mixed economy rather than an all-meat cartoon. Because those samples are not securely Southern Xiongnu households of 100 to 300, this card uses them as inherited background and refuses to print one universal frontier menu.

Dairy processing had a very long eastern-steppe history before the Southern polity. Milk from managed animals could become durable food through fermentation, but direct residues from a Southern Xiongnu kitchen in this interval are scarce. “They certainly drank this exact recipe” would be a tastier sentence than the evidence allows.

At Budongdou in Inner Mongolia, nine graves assigned by excavators to a Southern Xiongnu context held pottery, many iron objects and offerings including horse, ox and sheep skulls. Burial food and animals reveal ritual and wealth; they are not a photograph of Tuesday dinner or proof of equal access.

sections.title: Families, rank and children lived inside unequal worlds

items.text: Steppe communities often organized around families and clans that herded and hunted together. The Southern court’s marriage houses and ranked princes fit that wider pattern, but political kinship was not the whole household world. Sources barely record adoption, divorce, care work, typical family size or ordinary disagreements.

A paired man-and-woman burial at Budongdou makes one relationship archaeologically visible, but it does not identify their names, marriage rules or feelings. Other graves held single bodies, and status differed through goods and offerings. One cemetery cannot be promoted into a census of all Southern Xiongnu families.

Court sources name a queen mother, consorts, princes and powerful marriage clans, showing that elite women mattered in succession and distribution. They say much less about women who herded, made clothing, prepared food or raised children. Absence from the annals is a documentary bias, not evidence of inactivity.

Children could inherit very different futures. A chanyu’s son might be sent to Luoyang as a political hostage and receive classical training, while pastoral children learned animals, routes and tools through work. Both are education, but only the elite pathway enters surviving court narratives with names and titles.

Rank depended on royal birth, marriage connections, office and the size of a leader’s following. Farmers, craftworkers, captives, guards and pastoral dependents are harder to place precisely. The evidence supports hierarchy but not a complete class chart, and it certainly does not tell us where every child sat at supper.

sections.title: Homes, clothes and objects crossed cultural lines

items.text: No reviewed source provides a standard Southern Xiongnu house plan. Some families remained mobile; others lived near Han forts, commandery towns or later Fen-valley settlements. Archaeology shows several ways of living, so assigning everybody the same round tent, or the same tiled courtyard, would replace uncertainty with furniture.

Han northern frontier archaeology finds a four-level hierarchy of walled settlements shaped by imperial planning and local variation. Southern Xiongnu communities lived within this political landscape, but a Han county wall is not automatically their home. Administrative space and domestic identity must stay analytically separate.

Earlier elite Xiongnu graves at Noin-Ula preserved caftans, trousers, leggings, felt, fur and imported silk. They demonstrate skilled textile work and long exchange, not the exact wardrobe of a Southern Xiongnu shepherd two centuries later. Ordinary patched clothing is much less likely than luxury cloth to survive.

Budongdou’s pottery, iron goods and animal offerings mix practices scholars call Xiongnu with objects circulating through Han territory. The material record can show contact and skilled making without assigning a single ethnicity to every jar. Frontier objects had careers; they did not politely remain in modern museum categories.

Even “Ordos style” is a risky shortcut. A scholarly review warns that finds from multiple styles and sometimes different named groups have been bundled under broad labels. The atlas polygon’s Alxa location makes restraint even more necessary: attractive bronzes cannot repair a misplaced map or identify their owner by silhouette.

sections.title: Learning, health, play and an outside written voice

items.text: For most children, no Southern Xiongnu curriculum survives. Pastoral work required learning animal behavior, weather, water, routes, riding and social obligations; that is a reasoned inference from the economy, not proof of a fixed starting age or identical training for girls and boys. Homework sometimes had hooves.

Liu Yuan’s reported classical education belongs near the end of this card and near the top of society. His reading across canonical, historical and military texts shows elite cultural crossing under Jin. It cannot establish mass literacy, village classrooms or equal access for daughters and sons.

A study of 104 Xiongnu-period skulls and 1,394 teeth from Mongolia found caries and calculus, with regional variation and evidence for carbohydrate consumption. Teeth document illness more securely than treatment: no Southern Xiongnu medical handbook, healer’s kit, hospital or reliable cure list survives in the reviewed evidence.

The Book of Later Han says Southern assemblies met three times a year for sacrifices, state discussion and horse and camel races. That joins religion, politics and play in one elite gathering. It is wonderful evidence for organized sport, but it does not name children’s games or prove every village held the same event.

An Eastern Han chronicle records “單于歲祭三龍祠，走馬鬥橐駝，以為樂事。” Modern Mandarin: “Chányú suì jì Sān Lóng Cí, zǒu mǎ dòu tuótuó, yǐ wéi lèshì.” Translation: “Each year the chanyu sacrificed at the Three Dragons shrine, raced horses and held camel contests for amusement.” This is authentic Classical Chinese external testimony, not Xiongnu speech or an indigenous script.

sections.title: Water, toilets and an honest blank space

items.text: Water governed pasture movement, animals and settlement along the Yellow River and Fen valley, but the reviewed evidence does not identify a Southern Xiongnu well, pipe network or drinking-water rule for 100 to 300. A river on a historical map proves access to water, not purity, distance, ownership or who carried it.

A first-century Eastern Han tomb model in the Smithsonian shows a glazed latrine joined to a pigsty. It proves that such an arrangement was imaginable in Han China. It does not prove that Southern Xiongnu households used it, that the model copies one real building, or that waste handling was hygienically safe.

A rare Eastern Han mural at Yinan shows a railed privy, water container, urinal jar and a servant cleaning. A Dunhuang relay-station latrine yielded hygiene sticks, some with faecal traces. Both are valuable Han evidence from other settings; neither is a Southern Xiongnu toilet in Ordos or Shanxi.

No reviewed excavation securely identifies a Southern Xiongnu latrine, cesspit, drain or sewer for this interval. People necessarily managed waste, but mobile camps, frontier villages and elite compounds may have differed. Calling any convenient pit a toilet would be archaeology by hopeful sniffing, so the answer stays unknown.

Political collapse did not stop eating, herding, washing, caring for children or disposing of waste. It mostly changed who claimed taxes, hostages and military service. Daily continuities are historically likely, but exact routines remain unevenly documented because court annals followed chanyus and rebellions more eagerly than water buckets.

ending.text: The Southern chanyu office effectively ended in 216 when Cao Cao retained Huchuquan at court and reorganized Xiongnu communities into Five Divisions. Pastoral work, families, group names and military networks continued under Cao Wei and Western Jin, especially around Shanxi’s Fen valley. Liu Yuan’s later regime began in 304 and belongs to the separately indexed Han-Zhao story; Xianbei confederations were distinct powers, not renamed Southern Xiongnu. The atlas carries this id to 300, so the last 84 years describe supervised communities and institutional afterlives rather than an independent chanyu state.
